A new study suggests rising colorectal cancer deaths among adults under 50 are concentrated among people with lower educational attainment, highlighting broader issues related to healthcare access, lifestyle factors, and early detection.


## Introduction


Colorectal cancer was once considered a disease primarily affecting older adults. Today, however, that assumption no longer holds true. Over the past several decades, doctors and researchers have observed a troubling increase in colorectal cancer diagnoses and deaths among younger adults, prompting renewed concern among public health experts.


Recent research sheds new light on this trend. While overall death rates from colorectal cancer among adults under 50 have increased, the burden appears to be disproportionately affecting individuals without a four-year college degree. Researchers believe this disparity may reflect deeper issues related to healthcare access, income, environmental exposure, health literacy, and lifestyle factors rather than education itself.


The findings highlight an important public health challenge and raise questions about why some groups are being affected more severely than others.


## Study Reveals a Widening Divide


Researchers from the American Cancer Society examined federal mortality data involving more than 101,000 adults between the ages of 25 and 49 who died from colon or rectal cancer between 1994 and 2023.


Their analysis found that the overall colorectal cancer death rate for adults in this age range increased from approximately 3 deaths per 100,000 people to around 4 deaths per 100,000 over the 30-year period.


However, a closer look at the data revealed a striking difference between education groups.


Among individuals without a bachelor's degree, colorectal cancer death rates increased significantly, rising from roughly 4 deaths per 100,000 people to 5.2 per 100,000. In contrast, death rates among people holding a bachelor's degree or higher remained relatively stable at approximately 2.7 deaths per 100,000.


As a result, the mortality gap between less educated and college-educated Americans has nearly doubled since the mid-1990s.


## Why Education May Matter


Researchers emphasize that a college degree itself is unlikely to directly prevent cancer. Instead, education often serves as a marker for broader socioeconomic factors that influence health outcomes throughout a person's life.


People with higher educational attainment frequently have access to better-paying jobs, employer-sponsored health insurance, paid sick leave, and more flexible work schedules. These advantages can make it easier to schedule medical appointments, obtain preventive care, and seek evaluation when symptoms first appear.


Those without similar resources may delay medical visits because of financial concerns, lack of insurance coverage, or difficulty taking time away from work. In many cases, delayed diagnosis can result in cancer being discovered at a more advanced and less treatable stage.


## Health Literacy and Early Detection


Another factor researchers point to is health literacy, which refers to an individual's ability to understand health information and navigate healthcare systems effectively.


People with lower health literacy may be less familiar with colorectal cancer symptoms or may not recognize when specific warning signs require medical attention. They may also face challenges understanding screening recommendations or accessing appropriate healthcare services.


This issue is particularly important because colorectal cancer symptoms can initially seem mild or easily explained by less serious conditions. As a result, younger adults sometimes dismiss early warning signs, assuming cancer is unlikely at their age.


When symptoms are ignored or misunderstood, valuable time can be lost before treatment begins.


## Environmental and Lifestyle Influences


Researchers also suggest that environmental and lifestyle factors could help explain the growing disparity.


Communities with fewer economic resources often face greater exposure to environmental pollutants and may have reduced access to healthy food options, recreational facilities, and preventive health programs.


Diet has been a particular focus in colorectal cancer research. Previous studies have linked poor dietary habits, obesity, and high consumption of heavily processed foods with increased colorectal cancer risk. While scientists have not identified a single cause for the rise in younger adults, many experts believe dietary patterns likely play an important role.


Smoking rates also tend to be higher among populations facing economic hardship. In addition, chronic financial stress can contribute to long-term health problems through sustained inflammation and other biological changes associated with stress.


Taken together, these factors may create conditions that increase cancer risk while simultaneously making early diagnosis more difficult.


## A Growing Concern Across the United States


The American Cancer Society estimates that more than 158,000 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer this year, with over 55,000 deaths expected from the disease.


Perhaps most concerning is the changing age profile of patients. Nearly half of colorectal cancer diagnoses are now expected to occur in people younger than 65, representing a major shift from previous decades when the disease was largely concentrated among older adults.


The trend has attracted increasing attention from public health organizations and cancer specialists who are working to understand the underlying causes behind the rise.


## Screening Recommendations Have Changed


In response to mounting evidence of increasing colorectal cancer cases among younger adults, the American Cancer Society lowered the recommended starting age for routine screening from 50 to 45 in 2021.


Screening can help identify cancer at an earlier stage and may even detect precancerous growths before they become malignant. Early detection remains one of the most effective tools for improving survival outcomes.


Experts encourage eligible adults to discuss screening options with their healthcare providers, particularly if they have a family history of colorectal cancer or other risk factors.


## Warning Signs Should Not Be Ignored


Medical professionals continue to urge younger adults to take potential symptoms seriously regardless of age.


Common warning signs can include:


- Persistent changes in bowel habits
- Blood in the stool
- Ongoing abdominal discomfort or pain
- Unexplained weight loss
- Persistent fatigue
- A feeling that the bowel does not empty completely


Many younger colorectal cancer patients are diagnosed only after the disease has progressed because symptoms were attributed to less serious conditions or overlooked altogether.


Awareness of these warning signs may help encourage earlier evaluation and improve health outcomes.


## Conclusion


The latest research highlights more than a medical issue. It underscores a growing health inequality affecting younger adults across the United States. Rising colorectal cancer deaths appear to be concentrated among people facing socioeconomic disadvantages, suggesting that healthcare access, environmental conditions, lifestyle factors, and health education all play a role in determining outcomes.


While researchers continue investigating why colorectal cancer is becoming more common among younger populations, one message is already clear: early detection, symptom awareness, and improved access to preventive healthcare could save lives.
